speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Business Trusts Act 2004, or BTA, provides a framework for the governance of registered Business Trusts (BTs), which are enterprises that combine the characteristics of both a company and a trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The BTA also facilitates the use of BTs as listing vehicles and as a new asset class for investors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: But unlike a company that can only pay dividends out of its accounting profits, a key feature of a BT is the ability to pay dividends out of its cash profits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This makes it particularly suited to businesses with stable growth and high cash flow, such as infrastructure businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Many requirements in the BTA were adapted from the Companies Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill proposes updates to the BTA that are consistent with amendments that have been made to the Companies Act to enhance the regulatory framework for companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In addition, MAS has also identified other legislative amendments that are needed to maintain the robustness and relevance of the regulatory regime for business trusts registered under the BTA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: First, is to enhance transparency and corporate governance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: With these amendments, unlisted registered business trusts will be subject to the same transparency requirements as unlisted companies regarding their beneficial owners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These requirements will help to mitigate the risk of business vehicles being used for illicit purposes, regardless of whether they take the form of a company or a trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, directors of trustee-managers of registered business trusts are required to disclose conflicts of interest in transactions as well as their interests in the registered business trusts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The change is consistent with existing disclosure requirements that are applicable to CEOs of companies under the Companies Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It also sets out procedures for the appointment of a new auditor where the resigning auditor is the sole auditor, including a reserve power for MAS to make such an appointment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These requirements will allow MAS to prevent a listed BT or its subsidiary from being left without an auditor.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Through the application process, MAS may also be alerted to any potential breaches of the BTA and the Accountants Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is in line with provisions in the Companies Act in relation to auditors of public interest companies, which include listed companies and their subsidiaries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The second key area is to strengthen the rights of unit-holders of registered business trusts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, unit-holders holding at least 10% of the voting rights of unit holders present at a meeting have the power to call for a poll.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill also expands the scope of the statutory derivative action in the BTA to allow a unit-holder to apply to the Court for leave to commence arbitration on behalf of all unit holders of the BT or to intervene in an arbitration to which the BT is a party.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This amendment will align unit-holders' rights to bring a derivative action with that of shareholders under the Companies Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In addition, where an application to wind up a registered BT has been filed in Court, the Bill expands the range of orders that the Court may make, including an order to buy out the interests of one or more unit-holders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, a Court hearing such an application can only make an order for the registered BT to be wound up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The additional remedy helps to protect the rights of minority unit-holders as there may be cases where the company is still viable and it would be a more efficient solution for the majority to buy out the minority or vice versa.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The third key area is to improve the ease of doing business and to reduce administrative burden.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These include changes to simplify deadlines for annual general meetings (AGMs) and the filing of annual returns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, registered business trusts are required to hold their AGMs once every calendar year and not more than 15 months after the preceding AGM and are also required to file annual returns within one month after the AGM.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These requirements do not refer to the financial year end of the registered BT.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill will align these timelines with the business trust's financial year end.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Bill will also mirror amendments to the Companies Act to reduce the number of documents accompanying a set of financial statements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To facilitate electronic communications by registered business trusts, the Bill allows for electronic transmission of notices and documents with unit-holders' implied or deemed consent, in accordance with the trust deed of the registered BT.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Currently, a registered BT wishing to publish notices and documents on a website can only do so with its unit-holders' express consent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The amendments will help to increase efficiency in this regard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Business trusts are structurally similar to REITs in that both are trusts constituted by a trust deed and, unlike companies, are not legal persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Both are also usually managed by an external manager.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Unit-holders' ability to vote to remove the external manager is a fundamental safeguard against such risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: They will streamline regulatory requirements and reduce compliance costs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This will improve the efficiency and robustness of the BT regulatory regime, benefiting the industry and investors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Business trusts are a common structure for tapping on capital on the SGX.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The proposed amendments to strengthen governance of business trusts are welcomed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Public consultations not only show that the Government is keen to listen but they also help our Government agencies guard against blind spots they may have during the policy-making process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also thank MAS for publishing a response paper to this public consultation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This gives respondents the assurance that their feedback is heard loud and clear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first set of clarifications has to do with loans to directors for defending against proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, it is common for a defendant in criminal proceedings to be convicted on some charges and acquitted on others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, in civil proceedings, a defendant may succeed on certain heads of claim but not others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify how repayment should be treated in such cases?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the director be required to repay only part of the loan?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Alternatively, will the need for repayment be determined by whether the director has succeeded overall in the criminal or civil proceedings?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If this is the case, how will overall success be determined?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is this determined by the number of charges or claims, or the severity of the charges or claims that the director succeeds on?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second set of clarifications has to do with a trustee-managers' duties to maintain information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The scope of such duties is potentially very large.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, can	the Minister of State explain why the new section 52K, which enforces a similar requirement to disclose information, does not apply to such a person?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would be helpful to understand why the two sections, similar in their scope, do not apply the burden to the same groups of people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To the extent that these amendments further strengthen the Government's provisions in BTs, many of these which have already been incorporated into other Acts, they are welcome.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For my speech, I wish to speak about three issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will begin by touching on a number of concerns directly related to the various amendments proposed by the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Next, I will move on to discuss the implications that the Bill may have by further encouraging the BT structure for the economy at large.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Before I proceed, I wish to declare that I am the Chief Economist (Emeritus) of Thirdrock, a homegrown boutique wealth management and consultancy business.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Bill offers a host of amendments, some 124 pages worth, for an original Act that was just 14 pages longer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some of these strike me as unambiguously good; others just a little bad and yet others just a tad ugly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For this reason, the change is good and very much welcome.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, I would question the porting of certain amendments just because they have been stipulated in the Companies Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As this House is likely aware, BTs are distinct from either corporations or trusts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For that reason, certain advantages offered to either pure business enterprises or trusts may not be as applicable to a BT.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The new sections 27B and 27C of the Act allows the trustee manager to extend trust monies via a loan on specified terms to trust directors, akin to sections of the Companies Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One could credibly make an argument that directors of a firm are integral to its viability as a going concern and hence deserving of such support from the business entity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the case is much harder to make for a trust.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the very design of a trust is already one step removed from the principles to allow business decisions to be rendered sufficiently independently of the directors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As another example, the new section 52C vests on the MAS the ability to liquidate and deregister BTs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be fair, this strikes me as a fairly pedestrian change that is likely to be invaluable for operational purposes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, I wish to seek the assurance of the Minister, that the MAS will only exercise this power to wind up BTs judiciously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, it should already be clear with exercising this clause, that the trust is already clear defunct, rather than an exercise of this power as a means of regulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By the same token, I wish to ask the Ministry to clarify the channels of appeal available to a BT in the event that it receives a request to wind up from the MAS, if it were to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, these appropriations from the Companies Act while undeniably better at aligning the two, do not sufficiently respect the distinctions between the two business structures and therefore, I find them at risk of being a little bombastic, admittedly, just a little ugly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Third, there is a potential bad that I wish to highlight from promoting the BT structure, especially over and above a REIT structure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As industry observers are well aware, a BT is not constrained, in terms of the amount of leverage they are able to take on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, while some BTs, do explicitly state that their practices more closely imitate REIT guidelines, such as restraining the amount of leverage that they take on, these are merely self-regulating assurances which are not limited by the force of law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This vehicle offers greater flexibility in extracting value from cashflow generating assets over how distributions may be made and in structuring of assets under development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Undoubtedly, there are major reasons for their comparative popularity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I also recognise that the benefits of BT from the perspective of our position as an international financial centre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Making as many possible asset management instruments available strengthens our relative attractiveness as an international financial and wealth management centre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It also allows our financial sector professionals and population at large to germinate keener interest and understanding of the role that increasingly more complex financial instruments play in our domestic and financial and economic landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, there are potential risks to the expanding role of BTs insofar as our economy is concerned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I had already alluded to on, pointing out that BTs are legally unconstrained by loan-to-value requirements and hence may engender greater financial stability concerns as a result.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to touch on another, one that may carry more profound implications for the average worker in the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As Members of this House are undoubtedly aware, business entities, whether taking the form of companies or a trust, typically adhere to the rigours of maximising profits and shareholder value.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In a world unencumbered by non-monetary considerations, it would be difficult to fault either entity for being more brutal in imposing market discipline.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we know that companies, large and small, deviate from this so-called neoclassical ideal all the time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Enterprises in China and Japan often strive to preserve employment, either for reasons of social stability or corporate loyalty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: German businesses consider not just shareholder interests, but also stakeholder ones, with labour unions, routinely engage in workplace bargaining with management to deliver extra employment protections or social benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even here at home, this Government has frequently trumpeted the importance of tripartite negotiations to promote aggregate welfare within our corporate context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This begs the question of how BTs fit into this overall picture of stakeholder capitalism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If BTs increasingly become a favourite structure for managing large business asset holdings, would the additional distance between unit-holders and management afforded by the BT and by design, inadvertently undermine the ability of workers to engage in negotiations with management?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would we see greater willingness by BT-managed businesses to fire employees at the first whiff of a downturn?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What are the implications of more REITS and real estate-focused BTs for escalating rent and sales prices, if such structures were to proliferate?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the BT structure, as opposed to other forms of trusts, permit greater, proactive involvement of the trustee manager in the everyday firm operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If this enhanced interventionism is paired with more flagrant disregard for non-pecuniary objectives – perhaps, because of differences in the investment horizon – then I fear that directed action by the trustee managers or their proxies on corporate decisions may induce more cut-throat behaviour by these firms in favour of capital, to the detriment of labour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this allows the trustee manager to exercise greater discretion in how they would translate cashflow into returns and is, in fact, one of the attractive aspects of a BT, one is left to wonder if this distinction ends up promoting excess accumulation and in turn, exacerbating wealth inequality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This, of course, is a non-trivial matter, as this House is well aware.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Social inequality has been rated by Singaporeans as their third most pressing concern, just behind bread-and-butter issues like employment and healthcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This concern is especially acute among young Singaporeans who, perhaps predictably, feel like they have the greatest state in the yawning wealth gap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It has also been exacerbated by the influx of wealthy individuals from abroad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What I am suggesting here is that we can go one step further and further refine our existing system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I previously alluded to how we could do this in the context of my Adjournment Motion on wealth taxation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will now elaborate on this idea in greater detail.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While trusts may seem esoteric and limited to high net worth individuals, most of us would, in fact, be familiar with some form of trust.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most of us would have nominated beneficiaries to our insurance policies or CPF monies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Last year, this House also debated amendments to the Mental Capacity Act, which included extensive discussion of the Lasting Power of Attorney, which is a trust arrangement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Those of us lucky enough to have savings set aside in a unit trust will have some familiarity with such investment trusts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And of course, most of us have contributed to charities at some point in our lives and such philanthropic foundations are the cornerstone of trust institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, even without more involved estate planning, the average Singaporean would have some exposure to the notion of trust.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, those with more means will often rely on yet more sophisticated instruments to manage their estate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Private family trusts, as well as family offices are increasingly widespread here, allowing us to harness our global advantages as a wealth management centre.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Investment oriented trust, including unit trusts or REITs and BTs – the focus of our debate today – enable such assets to grow in a manner unencumbered by tax considerations prior to vesting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the national level, this has promoted a landscape where trust institutions have become ever more important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, in spite of this rapid growth in investment-oriented trusts, there are only little more than 400 philanthropic organisations and trusts in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I venture that we can go further in how we manage our trust institutions, to not only accentuate their supply side, the growing of assets within a trust, but also to foster their demand side and evolve them into grant-making institutions and thereby, build a stronger culture of philanthropy among the wealthier in our nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since Independence, our per capita income, adjusted for inflation, have increased almost 16-fold, from around 5,800 to around 91,000 last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We are, undeniably, no longer a developing country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, our philanthropic culture still retains the vestiges of economies that are far less advanced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our fiscal financing, while diversified, essentially relies on a regime of low income taxes, with charges and fees, which are regressive in nature, still playing a prominent role.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This goes beyond approaches currently favoured by this Government, such as public-private finance partnerships for infrastructure or the granting of the right to issue tax exempt receipts for Institutions of Public Character.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In many advanced economies, wealthy individuals fund a wide range of socially beneficial activities, from naming rights to hospitals and university buildings and even park benches, to setting up non-profit organisations dedicated to various causes, to establishing foundations that provide grants to groups aligned with the foundation's declared mandate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One wonders if our tax structure could be further refined to provide additional incentives for business trusts to also be involved in philanthropic activities as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In other jurisdictions, such activities are all often wholly unconstrained.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a result, it could give rise to perverse situations where a billionaire's favourite pastimes, such as art galleries or classical music concerts are financed through tax exemptions, while causes that benefit the poor remain relatively underfunded, or foundations could become indirect wealth accumulation vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could also encourage the development of fundraising and grant writing expertise in our domestic workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Besides potentially expanding a small cottage industry in the social sector, it could also increase the awareness of, and affinity towards important causes that are valuable to our society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my conversations with those in industry, I have been impressed by the complementarities that exists between the supply and demand sides of the story.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, many donor trusts and foundations, private banking clients and non-profits are served by the self-same assets and wealth management professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My hopes, Sir, is that trusts and foundations will eventually become a part of our nation's social fabric, that we will not just privilege certain trust structures, such as investments or business trusts, to the detriment of others that will enrich the life of our citizens as well as our economy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will first address specific questions raised in the Bill before tackling the broader questions on the relevance of BTs' structure and the trust foundations in the philanthropy landscape.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But I also wanted to say that, for the purposes of this amendment Bill that we focus very much on the core of what we are trying to do, which is to enhance the transparency and strengthen governance of Business Trusts(BTs).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And for many other topics, we can leave that on another day.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On the Bill, both Mr Louis Ng and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim raised questions on provisions that will seek to align the BTA with a regulatory regime for companies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked about the appropriateness of replicating the Companies Act's provisions in the BTA, as well as whether we need to strengthen the regulatory regime for business trusts relative to the regulatory regime for REITs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: BTs, as the Member had noted, is also meant to be an alternative business structure to companies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Hence, the regulatory regime for BTs is modelled after that of companies.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Similar to the Companies Act, the intention of the BTA is to set out requirements to protect, indeed, the fundamental rights of unit-holders of these registered business trusts and to set out the duties and accountability of the trustee-managers and their directors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And then on top of requirements that we have adapted from the Companies Act, MAS has also included relevant governance requirements from the REIT regime.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: BTs and REITs, of course, share a lot of structural similarity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For example, both are externally managed, as I had mentioned in my speech.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS has also taken reference from applicable REIT rules when reviewing the BTA, especially in areas where the risks are similar.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If you reference the requirements for REIT managers, MAS is also considering amending subsidiary legislation of the BTA to enhance independence requirements for directors of trustee-managers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS will be consulting on its suite of proposed amendments to subsidiary legislation of the BTA in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Just a few points about the fiduciary role of the directors of the trustee-manager.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The directors of a trustee-manager essentially perform the same fiduciary role as the directors of a company.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Hence, we are trying to align the BTA with the Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The provisions allowing loans to be given to directors of companies are also relevant to the directors of trustee-managers within the BTA.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On whether vehicles are trying to get away with easier regulations as regard to the BT versus REIT – companies, BTs and REITs are, in fact, all subject to corporate governance requirements.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Assets that do not fall neatly under a REIT structure can be included in a company structure.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is important that we have these proper rules and consistent rules for both companies and BTs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And that is why, again, going back to the fundamentals, that is why we are aligning the BTA to the Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On section 52, it is an existing provision that MAS may apply to a Court, to appoint a liquidator to wind up, and thereafter, deregister a defunct BT.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The new section 52B provides for any persons with reasonable cause, that the BT should not be deregistered to object when MAS issues a notice of its intention to apply to Court for liquidation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The context of section 52 is actually for a defunct BT, but it is actually not for still functioning BTs – just to clarify that point, which is quite important.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Member, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also mentioned about the distance between trustee-managers in a BT, and unit-holders or stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The trustee-manager, in this regard, has to manage businesses and operations, just in the same way as the board or the management of companies and has to similarly consider the interest of key stakeholders, in order for the business to be successful.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Again, going back to it, is really aligning both.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are differences between REITs, as well as BTs and that is why although they are structurally similar, some of the provisions, we have to regard them as separate as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will address other points with regards to trust and REITs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: REITs are investment funds which are obviously subjected to investment guidelines and are intended to specifically hold income-producing properties.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They are business structures which can hold the wide range of assets.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned many of the 18 that he raised earlier on.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, they do hold a wide range of assets but they are not limited to real estate, although many that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim raised appear to be linked to real estate, but they can also operate active businesses.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The two regulatory regimes cannot, therefore, be equalised.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS will also regularly review the regulatory regime for BTs and will make appropriate refinements to ensure that the regime remains robust and also meet the market needs, as and when it is required.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Louis Ng raised a few questions relating to loans by trustee-managers to their directors for defending against proceedings or regulatory actions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Ng also asked about the difference in treatment between loans made to directors for defending against civil and criminal proceedings, compared to loans to directors for defending against regulatory actions.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The difference in treatment also follows from equivalent provisions in the Companies Act and it can also be found in the UK Companies Act as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked for clarification, whether repayment will be required in situations not specified in the Bill, such as if charges are withdrawn.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Loans, by their very nature, are expected to be repaid according to the terms of the loan agreement unless otherwise agreed with the lender.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: While the Bill will not require trustee-managers to include terms in their loan agreement for repayment of loans under circumstances other than those specified in the Bill, trustee-managers can still choose to include such terms as they deem appropriate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For repayment terms that are required by the Bill, Mr Louis Ng further asked how these should apply where a loan was granted to a director to defend criminal or civil proceedings and a conviction or judgment against the director was only obtained for some, but not all, of the charges or heads of claims.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The next set of questions Mr Louis Ng raised relates to the transparency requirements for unlisted business trusts regarding their registrable controllers, or controllers in short.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: He asked what would constitute "reasonable steps" for the purpose of a trustee-managers' discharge of their obligations to identify controllers of a BT.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Under ACRA's guidance, a company is regarded as having taken "reasonable steps" if it sends out a notice at least annually to each member and each director of the company, unless the person has already provided it with the requisite information.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Louis Ng further asked about the differing burdens placed on a controller versus a person who knows or ought to know the identity of a controller.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For brevity, I will refer to the latter as third parties.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Bill requires both controllers and third parties to provide information to the trustee-manager when served with a notice to do so.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In addition, controllers are required to notify trustee-managers of their particulars, such as the dates they became controllers of the BTs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: However, third parties are not under similar obligations to furnish information on a controller unless they have been asked to do so by the trustee-managers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The differing requirements are intended to balance between requiring trustee-managers to maintain a complete register of its controllers and the burden to third parties.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The duty to notify the trustee-manager of a controller's beneficial ownership of the BT falls naturally on the controller himself, as he is the primary source of information about his own interests in the BT.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The same cannot be said for third parties, who are one step removed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Requiring a third party to provide the trustee-manager with information on another person, the controller, without being asked to do so would impose an excessive burden on the third party.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Nevertheless, where a third party is served a notice by the trustee-manager to provide information on a controller, he would be clearly informed that the information is required of him.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: He would therefore be obligated to provide the information in this situation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Business trusts are by design suitable for businesses, as I have mentioned in my earlier speech, that have high cash flows and also stable growth.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They add to the array of many alternative structures for businesses to organise themselves in a manner that meets their operating and fundraising needs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As for Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's suggestions to support a culture of philanthropy, they extend quite beyond the scope of the BTA, as I have mentioned earlier, but we will be happy to take those questions as matters for further study where relevant.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will also just mention that one of the strategies under MAS' Financial Services Industry Transformation Map (ITM) 2025, is to help to develop Singapore into Asia's centre for philanthropy and MAS will provide support in line with this ITM.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, last week, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a number of measures that we are studying, including reviewing our tax incentive structures and schemes to see how we can encourage family offices to do more philanthropic giving and to support the local philanthropic ecosystem, by structuring their giving through local charities and also non-profit entities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Just on another point by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim on taking a more interventionist approach to direct high net worth wealth to fund specific causes that are aligned with Singapore's interest, the approach thus far has been to enhance just the overall ecosystem to encourage high net worth individuals to conduct their giving activities in Singapore, effectively just to build the culture of philanthropy until so when these offices and these structures come to Singapore encourage them to give locally as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I also want to just share as a final point that this is not very unique to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, apart from Singapore, there are few other jurisdictions where BTs are also used as corporate vehicles.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Australia, Hong Kong, Canada have business vehicles quite similar to our BTs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But, of course, our own BT regime has its own legal framework with very clear rules that are specifically tailored to the features of our Bts.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, it was developed to be as close to a company as possible, as they are intended to be an alternative structure to companies so that they have that flexibility.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For example, Malaysia's BT regime is also quite similar to that in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are also other jurisdictions – Australia, Hong Kong and Canada, for example – that have different structures, but they have their own regulatory regimes suited to their own ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In short, by amending this Bill, the Bill will contribute towards a strong, a robust and transparent regulatory framework for businesses and investors, and also support Singapore's business competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.52 pm until 4.15 pm.
